the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.bio: Podcast: Why Every AI Agent Needs Its Own Computer | Ivan Burazin (Daytona)

html_en:
While enterprises remain skittish about energy infrastructure and designers question whether AI agents truly understand craft, the industry is doubling down on creating the foundational compute architecture that will power our autonomous future.

The Computer for Every Agent

The most fascinating development today comes from Daytona's Ivan Burazin, who makes a compelling case that we're thinking about AI agents all wrong. In a detailed conversation on Matt Turck's MAD Podcast, Burazin argues that every AI agent needs its own dedicated computer — what the industry calls a "sandbox."
"When I think about agents, I think of them as digital knowledge workers. And to do anything as a knowledge worker, you do need a computer,"
Burazin explains. Watch/Listen: Why Every AI Agent Needs Its Own Computer The reasoning becomes clear when you consider security. Burazin recounts asking Claude to fetch bank data during a board meeting:
"It was like, oh yeah, just log in and give me access. I'm like, log in and give me a no. I will not give you access. Right away fundamentally for me that was like broke the entire thesis of it."
His solution? Give the agent its own machine, complete with dedicated accounts and phone numbers for 2FA. It's a radical shift from thinking of agents as software features to viewing them as digital employees who need their own workspace.

The Reality Check on AI Development

While the infrastructure vision expands, developers are running into practical limits. Peter Yang captures the current frustration perfectly:
"How do people even do AI hackathons these days you're just sitting around waiting for the agents half of the time?"
His observation reflects a broader challenge — AI development cycles are increasingly constrained by model response times rather than human coding speed. Yang also highlights a design problem many are discovering:
"TIL having AI just start making screens without a design system or components is a sure fire path to slop. Maybe those designers were onto something"
This insight suggests that effective AI collaboration still requires human-designed guardrails and systematic thinking.

Infrastructure Wars and Market Dynamics

The infrastructure conversation extends beyond compute to fundamental questions about market access. Nikunj observes that
"Every single large company with data walls realizing it's time to go headless (or essentially die).. If you gatekeep your systems for humans, you'll most likely be 100x less valuable!"
His prediction reflects the pressure on enterprises to open APIs for agent access or risk obsolescence. Meanwhile, Garry Tan pushes back against energy infrastructure resistance, arguing that "The electricity NIMBYs strike again. Have you guys heard of markets?" The tension between AI's energy demands and local opposition is becoming a critical bottleneck.

Enterprise Adoption Accelerates

Despite infrastructure challenges, enterprise adoption is moving faster than expected. Dan Shipper shares a telling anecdote:
"Guy in the chair next to me leans over and says his company just bought 1,300 Claude seats. 2026 is wild"
This casual barbershop conversation reveals how AI tools are moving from experimental to operational at scale. The most significant news came from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who announced "Codex in the ChatGPT mobile app!" — bringing computer control capabilities directly to mobile users' fingertips.

The Specialization Question

Box CEO Aaron Levie offers perhaps the most nuanced take on how AI will reshape professional roles. While acknowledging that AI lets people explore adjacent functions more easily, he argues that specialization will ultimately deepen rather than disappear:
"My bet is that AI enhances specialization even further, even if a few roles collapse into each other, and the future toolchain and craft of the specialist will be much higher leverage and output far greater than anyone else as a hobbyist in that function."
His thread suggests we're in a temporary period of role confusion that will eventually settle into new, more specialized forms. The day's conversations reveal an industry grappling with fundamental questions about compute architecture, professional identity, and market access — all while racing to build the infrastructure for an agent-powered future that's arriving faster than anyone expected.
html_zh:
当传统企业遇到AI，幽默往往比严肃更有效果——正如SAP在迈阿密AI会议上的意外收获所证明的那样，同时技术圈在重新思考AI时代工作角色的重新定义。

当嘲讽变成商机：企业AI转型的意外契机

企业AI转型的故事往往从最不经意的地方开始。@swyx在推特上分享了一个有趣的故事：
"显然在@AIEMiami会议上，geoff抱怨@SAPConcur是死软件，而台下恰好坐着一位SAP员工，他邀请geoff到SAP为6800名员工的AI转型提供建议。简而言之，他嘲笑了SAP，而SAP...同意了"
这个故事折射出一个更深层的现象：传统企业正在积极寻求外部视角来推动AI转型，即使这种视角最初是批判性的。企业领导层越来越意识到，内部的惯性思维可能是数字化转型的最大障碍。 与此相呼应，@nikunj观察到了一个更广泛的趋势："每一家拥有数据壁垒的大型公司都意识到是时候去无头化（或者本质上就是死亡）了...如果你为人类用户设置系统门槛，你很可能价值缩水100倍！"

AI开发的现实困境：等待与设计的平衡

AI开发的日常现实远比想象中更复杂。Peter Yang在推特上提出了一个尖锐问题：
"现在的人们是怎么参加AI黑客马拉松的？你大部分时间都在坐着等AI代理完成工作？"
这个观察揭示了一个有趣的悖论：AI工具提高了效率，但也改变了工作的节奏。开发者发现自己从主动编码者变成了AI的管理者和等待者。 同时，Yang还发现了另一个重要问题："让AI在没有设计系统或组件的情况下开始制作界面，肯定会导致糟糕的结果。也许那些设计师确实有道理" 这提醒我们，AI工具的强大不能替代基础的设计原则和系统性思考。

角色重新定义：专业化还是泛化？

Box CEO Aaron Levie对这一趋势进行了深度思考：
"我们正处在一个一切都感觉在角色间变得混乱的时期，因为AI让你更容易探索其他职能的邻接领域...我的预测是，AI会进一步增强专业化，即使一些角色会相互融合，专业人士的未来工具链和技能水平会比任何人作为业余爱好者在该功能上的表现要高得多。"

技术突破：从终端到移动端的AI体验

技术创新正在让AI变得更加无处不在。Vercel的CEO Guillermo Rauch展示了一个令人印象深刻的功能：
"你可以在终端直接渲染图像：▲ ~/ npx ai-cli image 'a vercel ai sdk diagram'"
与此同时，Sam Altman宣布了Codex正式登陆ChatGPT移动应用，这标志着AI编程助手从桌面走向移动端的重要一步。 Replit的CEO Amjad Masad也带来了好消息，在与苹果解决争议后，"我们与苹果达成了协议，4个月来首次发布了我们的应用"。他们还推出了一个大胆的功能："你在Replit之外编写了网站？没关系...我们将让你导入它并获得免费的移动应用。是的，免费移动应用！"

基础设施革命：每个AI代理都需要自己的计算机

在最新的MAD播客中，Daytona的CEO Ivan Burazin分享了一个基础设施层面的重要观点：
"当我思考代理时，我把它们看作数字知识工作者。作为知识工作者要做任何事情，你确实需要一台计算机...我的论点是每个代理至少需要一个沙箱，有时需要更多。"
Burazin还分享了一个生动的例子，说明为什么代理需要隔离的计算环境：
"我会问Claude，你能去从我们的银行获取数据吗？然后它说，'哦好的，只需登录并给我访问权限。'我说，登录并给我...不，我不会给你访问权限。这立即从根本上为我打破了整个理论。所以你给它自己的机器。"
在AI快速发展的时代，我们看到的不仅是技术的进步，更是工作方式和商业模式的根本性变化。从SAP的开放态度到开发者的新挑战，从角色定义的重新思考到基础设施的创新需求，每一个变化都在重塑我们对AI未来的理解。正如Dan Shipper在理发店的对话中感受到的那样："2026年真是疯狂"——AI已经深入到了每个人的日常生活中。
